title: CAPABILITIES AND LIMITATIONS OF LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
explain_beginner: This paper takes stock of what today's large language models, the AI systems behind tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, can do well and where they still fall short, aimed at helping people choose and use these tools more wisely. Rather than running new experiments, the authors reviewed how these models evolved, explained how the underlying transformer architecture and its attention mechanism work, and then compared the three named chatbots directly. They describe the attention mechanism as a major breakthrough behind the recent leap in AI language capability, enabling real gains in productivity and in working with text-based tasks across many industries. At the same time, they caution that picking the right model for a specific job is genuinely difficult, given how complex these architectures are and how much training data they require, and that users need to stay cautious about trusting everything a model generates. Their practical suggestion is that open-source models or third-party integrations can sometimes be a more accessible or controllable alternative to the big commercial chatbots.
explain_business: For a business deciding how to deploy chatbot-style AI, this paper's main practical value is a reminder, not a new capability, that ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini differ enough in behavior that a one-size-fits-all choice is likely to be suboptimal, so matching a specific model to a specific task is worth the evaluation effort rather than defaulting to whichever tool is most familiar. The authors explicitly flag output trustworthiness as a caveat that any deployment should account for, meaning human review remains necessary rather than optional for consequential tasks. They also point to open-source models or third-party integrations as viable alternatives worth considering, particularly where cost, customization, or data control matter more than using a leading commercial chatbot directly. Nothing in this paper indicates a new capability jump or new risk beyond what is already known about these three chatbots, it is best read as a grounding reference for teams new to evaluating LLM options, rather than as evidence for updating existing deployment or procurement decisions.
explain_practitioner: This is a literature review and comparative analysis rather than an empirical study with a novel benchmark. The authors trace the evolution of large language models, walk through transformer architecture and the attention mechanism underlying it, review typical training pipelines including data collection, preprocessing, and neural network selection, and then compare three widely used chatbots, ChatGPT, Claude AI, and Gemini AI, on their practical behavior and characteristics. The result that matters most for practitioners is the framing of attention as a pivotal architectural advance enabling modern LLM capability, paired with a caution that no single model is universally best, each has distinct strengths and weaknesses that must be matched to the task at hand. The paper's own noted limitation is that selecting and configuring the right model for a given use case is a genuinely difficult process, complicated by architectural complexity and heavy training-data requirements, and that outputs still require caution regarding trustworthiness. As a secondary point, the authors suggest open-source models or third-party integrations as more practical or lower-risk alternatives to the major commercial systems in some situations.
